39: Hosts in the United States hire mobile bars for three kinds of events: weddings, corporate events and private celebrations. Search data shows the interest is real but niche. People look up "mobile bar business" about 480 times a month and "dry hire mobile bar" about 390 times (DataForSEO, October 2026), and many of those searches come from people thinking about starting one. We do not quote a market size, because no source we could open gives a reliable one. What matters is local: how many weddings, venues, offices and event planners sit within an hour or two of your storage unit. This plan describes a mobile bar company that serves all three groups without owning a bar or holding an alcohol inventory.
40: The concept is a mobile bar and bartending service sold as dry hire (your client buys the alcohol; you bring the bar, the bartenders and everything else). We tow a converted bar trailer to the event, and a portable bar covers the second crew and ballrooms the trailer cannot enter. Our W-2 bartenders hold their state alcohol server certification and pour a short list of signature cocktails, with mixers, garnishes, ice and cups included. We handle setup and breakdown, and we send the host a shopping list so they buy the right amount of alcohol and nothing more. The owner's own pickup tows the trailer, so there is no vehicle on the startup list. What we sell is a bar that runs itself, not a drink.
41: The total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} of capex plus {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. The largest lines are the used bar trailer and its conversion, the wrap and bar facade, the portable bar, the glassware and coolers, and the website and photos that sell the first weddings. There is no alcohol inventory to finance, because the host buys it. The cash needed at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. We cover it with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, a size that fits within an SBA Microloan, which is capped at $50,000. Lenders still decide case by case, so treat the structure as a starting point for your own conversation.
42: In year 1 we plan {{eventos_a1}} events with an average of {{invitados_evento}} guests at {{precio_invitado}} per guest, excluding sales tax and alcohol. That adds up to {{ventas_a1}} in revenue, growing to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3. Year-1 EBITDA is {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales, the business breaks even at {{equilibrio_eventos}} events a year, and the lowest debt service coverage over the loan term is {{dscr_min}}. Read these numbers for what they are. They describe a full-time operator with two crews and a marketing budget, in the upper quarter of the market, not the average mobile bar. Section 3 shows what a typical first year looks like.
43: The founding team is an owner who works as lead bartender and also sells, a second-crew lead bartender on part-time W-2 hours, a pool of event bartenders paid by the hour, and barbacks who handle loading and setup. That makes {{plantilla_puestos}} people, or {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents, and the hours rise and fall with the number of events. Replace this paragraph with your own background: a lender wants to see who has worked behind a bar and who has sold events. The plan shows that a mobile bar can start with controlled risk, as long as every event is quoted, deposited and staffed on purpose.
46: Our clients buy a bar that works without them having to think about it, not a round of drinks. The first group is couples planning a wedding or a rehearsal dinner, who want one vendor for the bar, the bartenders and the cleanup. The second is companies, where an office manager or an event planner needs a holiday party or a client event handled without surprises. The third is private hosts: milestone birthdays, anniversaries, graduations and housewarmings. All three care about the same things: a bar that is ready before the first guest arrives, bartenders who pour responsibly, and a quote with no surprises. The difference is the sales cycle. Couples book once and months ahead, while companies and repeat hosts come back.
47: Our value proposition rests on three pillars. First, zero complexity for the host. The bar, the bartenders, glassware, ice, mixers and garnishes arrive together, and setup and breakdown are included, so nobody on the host's side has to run to the store at 4 p.m. Second, a drink menu that fits the event. Every bar carries a short list of signature cocktails and at least one mocktail, so guests who do not drink are not left with a can of soda. Third, a shopping list that tells the host exactly which bottles to buy and how many, based on guest count and event length. That keeps them from overbuying and gives us a reason to be called the easy option. Each pillar lets us charge for the service, not for the pour.
48: We quote bar packages per guest, excluding sales tax and alcohol, and the average is {{precio_invitado}}. With {{invitados_evento}} guests per event, the average event brings in {{ventas_evento}}. Each package also has an hourly equivalent, so a host with a short event or a small crowd can compare it with a bartender-only quote. Add-ons cover travel fees, an extra hour of service, glassware, champagne service and specialty bars. A deposit of 30% holds the date, which is the typical level Check Cherry reports. Voluntary gratuity stays with the bartenders and out of our margin. In dry hire we never charge for individual drinks.
49: What sets us apart is the specialty bar. A mimosa bar for a brunch wedding, an espresso martini bar for the late-night hour, a tiki bar for a summer party, a speakeasy setup for a corporate evening or a gin bar with garnish options turns the bar into part of the entertainment. Each one carries a surcharge, because it needs extra supplies, a sign and a bartender who knows the routine. We also print the drink menu with the couple's names or the company's logo, which guests photograph and share. These are the details that planners remember when a client asks for a vendor recommendation.
50: The pricing calculator in this kit builds three packages. A full bar in dry hire serves signature cocktails, mocktails and the host's beer and wine. A limited bar in dry hire is the entry package, usually beer and wine plus one signature cocktail. A full bar with a license is the third option, and it only applies if you work with a licensed partner or hold the license yourself. Each package has a minimum booking, so small events do not lose money on the trailer and the crew, and an extra hour of service is priced separately. The calculator builds the quote from your own costs, so the price per guest is never a guess.
53: Demand for mobile bars in the United States comes from the client side. Check Cherry analyzed 1,334 confirmed bookings and reports a median price of $750 per event, excluding alcohol and tips, with the middle half between $450 and $1,275. Those are prices for the market as it is, and they sit well below the {{ventas_evento}} of our example. Buyers also search for the service itself, with "mobile bartending services" and "bartending services" each at about 1,300 searches a month (DataForSEO, October 2026). We quote no total market size. What counts for a new operator is how many weddings, offices and venues you can reach from your base.
54: Weddings are the most valuable segment. Check Cherry reports a median of $675 for a four-hour event and $1,063 for 101 to 150 guests, so price rises with both the guest count and the time on the clock. Couples also book early, with a median of 62 days between the booking and the event, and the calendar is tight: peak wedding season runs May to June and September to October, and those are the dates that fill first. These clients compare packages, read reviews on The Knot and Zola, and often ask for a tasting before they sign, so the first conversation matters more than any ad.
55: Corporate events and private parties add weekday and winter volume. Companies book holiday parties in December, client receptions, team events and product launches, usually through an office manager or a planner who needs an invoice and a certificate of insurance. Private hosts book birthdays, anniversaries, graduations and retirement parties. The weekend still dominates: according to Check Cherry, about 85% of bookings fall between Friday and Sunday, and half of them on a Saturday. A company that books a Thursday evening is useful because it fills a night that would otherwise stay empty.
56: The example case mixes the three groups. It assumes 60 weddings, 45 corporate events and 55 private parties, which is a kit estimate and not market data. Weddings are 37.5% of the events and about 48% of the sales, because they have more guests and run longer. The calendar is uneven, and the example opens in March, so Month 1 is March. Check Cherry puts October at about 13% of the year, May at 12.4% and January at 3.8%. Rotate the curve to your own opening month and replace the shares with what your first bookings suggest. Your local calendar will differ, especially in warm climates where winter is less quiet.
57: A few trends are worth watching, without leaning on numbers we cannot source. Mocktails and zero-proof drinks are now expected on a drink menu, not an afterthought. Specialty bars give planners something to show on social media. Personalized drink menus and a bar that matches the event's colors are easy to offer and hard to copy at scale. We treat these as reasons to design the bar well, not as claims about growth.
58: Demand carries risks the plan should name. Wedding season is short, so a slow spring can leave a gap that fall cannot fully fill. Hosts cancel or shrink the guest count late, which is why the deposit and the cancellation terms matter. Be realistic about the first year: according to Check Cherry, the median mobile bar with a year of history did 3 events, and the top 10% did about 39. The example case is a full-time operator with two crews and a marketing budget, not the average. If your pessimistic scenario ends the year with {{pesimista_caja}} in cash, read that line as the point where you need a smaller launch or more savings.
61: Before you price anything, map who competes within an hour or two of your storage unit. The list usually includes other mobile bars and bartending services with a wedding reputation, venues that run their own bar, licensed caterers that include a bar in the package, and individual bartenders who list themselves on gig marketplaces. Each one answers a different need, and writing them down shows where a small, well-reviewed mobile bar with a trailer has room.
62: The five forces look like this for a mobile bar. Supplier power is low: trailers, bar equipment and mixers are plentiful and easy to switch, and the host buys the alcohol. Buyer power is moderate, because clients compare quotes and reviews on The Knot, Zola and GigSalad, but a clear proposal and a good tasting build loyalty. The threat of substitutes is real, since a venue bar, a licensed caterer or a friend with a keg can replace us on a small budget. Rivalry peaks in wedding season, when local bars compete for the same Saturdays. The threat of new entrants is high at the low end. Check Cherry notes that a portable bar can start from around $1,000, but a converted trailer, insurance, certified bartenders and a review history take time and cash, which separates serious operators from weekend hobbyists.
63: Direct competitors are other mobile bars and bartending services that serve the same guest counts and the same venues, plus any bartender-only service that undercuts your price. Indirect competitors are venues with an in-house bar, licensed caterers and hosts who simply hire one friend to pour. To compare yourself fairly, line up price per guest or per hour, what the price includes, the number of bartenders, the minimum booking and the reviews on The Knot, WeddingWire, Zola, GigSalad and Google. Then decide where you win: the trailer, the signature cocktails, the response time or the clarity of the quote. Say it in one sentence and use it everywhere.
64: The barriers to entry are moderate and depend on the model. A portable bar, a few bartenders and a set of tools can start from about $1,000, according to Check Cherry, which is why the low end is crowded. A converted trailer raises the bar: it needs capital, a tow vehicle, parking and a build that passes any county inspection. Insurance is the second barrier, because general liability usually excludes alcohol, so you add liquor liability and carry commercial auto and workers' compensation. Venues ask for a certificate of insurance naming them as additional insured. Alcohol rules also change by state, so check yours before you sell a single package.
65: Five factors decide whether a mobile bar succeeds. The first is reliability: arriving early, setting up cleanly and being ready before the first guest. The second is responsible service, with certified bartenders who cut off guests politely and keep the host protected. The third is reputation, built on reviews after every event. The fourth is relationships with venues and wedding planners, who steer many bookings and remember who made their day easier. The fifth is a bar that looks good in photos, because couples and planners post them. A small operator that gets these five right can win work from larger competitors.
66: The SWOT analysis for this concept is straightforward. Strengths: no alcohol inventory or license to carry in dry hire, a trailer that photographs well, signature cocktails and specialty bars that justify a higher price, and W-2 bartenders who are trained and insured. Weaknesses: dependence on a few lead bartenders, limited capacity on peak Saturdays with only two crews, and an uneven calendar. Opportunities: venues and planners with preferred vendor lists, companies that repeat every December, and hosts who value a shopping list and a clear quote. Threats: a serious incident at an event, late cancellations, changes to state alcohol rules, and gig marketplaces that push prices down.
69: Our marketing strategy follows two funnels. Weddings have a long cycle: the couple finds us online, asks for a quote, attends a tasting and signs months before the date. Companies and private hosts have a shorter, repeat-driven cycle: one smooth party leads to the next booking and to a recommendation inside the same office or friend group. We treat each funnel differently in message and in channel, but both rest on the same promise: a bar that is ready on time, staffed by people who pour responsibly and look after the guests.
70: The website is our main sales tool, because clients check it before they call. It shows our packages with "from" prices per guest, photos of real setups, a sample drink menu and a short quote form that asks for the date, the venue, the guest count and the event length. Beside it, a complete Google Business Profile with photos, service areas and recent reviews puts us in front of people who search for a mobile bar nearby. Instagram and Pinterest carry photos of the trailer, the specialty bars and the signature cocktails. We answer every review within a day, positive or negative.
71: Directories bring in qualified leads when a profile is complete. For weddings, The Knot, WeddingWire and Zola are where couples compare vendors, read reviews and send quote requests, so a full profile with photos and packages is worth the effort. GigSalad, The Bash and Thumbtack reach hosts for parties and corporate events, at the cost of a fee: the workbook models {{marketplace_comision}} on the {{marketplace_pct}} of sales that comes through them. We use marketplaces to find first-time clients and then invite the best ones to book direct next time.
72: Alliances do more than ads. Visit venues and ask to be added to their preferred vendor lists, since a venue that recommends you sends bookings without any advertising cost. Introduce yourself to wedding planners and coordinators, photographers and DJs, who meet the same couples and refer each other. Bring a sample drink menu and a certificate of insurance to every visit. Book a table at a local bridal show, where couples come ready to hire. Follow each contact with an email within a day. A steady rhythm of small contacts each week usually beats one big campaign.
73: Tastings and menu consultations are our closest step to the sale, so we budget for them as a line in the profit and loss statement. We offer them to serious prospects, mainly couples and larger corporate events, with two or three signature cocktails and a printed proposal. The proposal sets out the packages, the number of bartenders, the add-ons, the price per guest, the deposit and the cancellation terms. After the tasting we follow up within a day. Once the client accepts, we send the service agreement and collect the deposit to hold the date.
74: The best marketing happens after the event. We ask for a review within a few days, while the host still remembers the night, and we send a short thank-you with a photo when the client agrees. Companies that book every December get a simple rebooking process, with last year's drink menu saved and one named contact. We ask happy hosts for an introduction to a friend planning a party or a colleague who books events. Repeat clients and referrals cost less to win than any new lead.
75: The example budgets {{marketing_anual}} a year for marketing, mainly for directory listings, photography, bridal shows and a modest amount of search advertising. We track every lead back to its source (website, The Knot, WeddingWire, Zola, GigSalad, venue or referral) and calculate the marketing cost per event won. If a channel books events at a lower cost, it gets more of the budget, and if it does not, we stop. Review the numbers each quarter and adjust.
